sentences.text: The animal belongs to the genus Barosaurus, with the only valid species being Barosaurus lentus.
Barosaurus affinis is considered a synonym of Barosaurus lentus.
Adult Barosaurus measured about 25 to 27 meters in length and weighed between 12 and 20 metric tons.
Compared to Diplodocus, Barosaurus had a relatively longer neck but a shorter tail, possessing 16 cervical vertebrae, which are more numerous than those of Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.
The Royal Ontario Museum Barosaurus specimen is nicknamed "Gordo" after curator Gordon Edmunds.
Barosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1890.

The first Barosaurus remains were discovered in 1889 in the Morrison Formation of South Dakota by Isabella R. Ellerman and excavated by Othniel Charles Marsh and John Bell Hatcher; the holotype specimen initially consisted of four tail vertebrae found by Ellerman.
Specimens of Barosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation in Utah and Montana, with potential fossils reported from Colorado, Wyoming, and Oklahoma.

A 2016 preprint by Mike Taylor and Mathew Wedel argued that Barosaurus cervical vertebrae allowed significant lateral neck flexibility but restricted vertical flexibility, suggesting Barosaurus did not primarily feed on vegetation high off the ground.
A 1992 study suggested that Barosaurus would have needed a heart weighing 1.6 tons, which is about one-tenth of its body weight, to pump blood up its long neck.
Barosaurus lived in present-day North America during the Late Jurassic period, specifically during the Kimmeridgian stage, approximately 152 to 150 million years ago.
The Morrison Formation environment where Barosaurus lived featured a floodplain with hot summers and moderate winters.
It is noted that late 20th-century depictions of Barosaurus as a short-tailed sauropod with a U-shaped neck are considered errors based on a specific artistic interpretation.
It is debated whether a specimen from the Kadsi Formation in Zimbabwe represents Barosaurus, as its referral is doubtful due to poor preservation and it may instead be Tornieria.

There is a debate regarding sauropod posture, with traditional views depicting a sprawled gait and later studies suggesting necks held high to graze tall trees; however, studies conclude that the neutral posture of Diplodocus was close to horizontal, leading scientists like Kent Stevens to argue that Barosaurus did not raise its head much above shoulder level.
